items.prose: An interviewer sets a leaderboard and then follows up. `add_score(player, delta)` adds `delta`, which may be negative, to a player's score. `top(k)` returns the sum of the `k` highest scores. The driver `run_board` is hidden, with rows `[0, player, delta]`, `[1, k]` and `[2, player]`.

widget.how: Check runs 4 hidden tests: a score that changes, an empty board, and a `top` larger than the board.

feedback.correct: A dict of scores, sorted when `top` is asked.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1: player 2 gains 51, so the top two are 73 and 107.
byKey.test-2: Test 2: player 1 adds 5 and 7, so the score is 12.
byKey.test-3: Test 3: an empty board sums to 0.
byKey.test-4: Test 4: with 3 players, `top(5)` sums all three.

explain.text: Keep one score per player in a dict. `top(k)` sorts the scores from the largest and sums the first `k`. A `k` larger than the board just sums everyone.

parts.question: The interviewer says there are 100,000 players and 2,000 `top(10)` calls. What do you change?

options.text: Keep the scores ordered, updating them on each change
Sort once at the start and then never update the order
options.why: You sorted once. Scores change, so the order goes stale.

options.text: Use a list of pairs instead of a dict, sorted on each call
options.why: You changed the container. Sorting a list every time costs the same.

options.text: Recompute `top` only on the first call, then reuse it
options.why: You cached the first answer. Later calls would return old totals.

feedback.correct: Keep the scores ordered, so a query reads 10 entries.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each query costs now.

byKey.b: A sort done once is out of date after the next score change.
byKey.c: A list sorted on every call costs as much as a dict sorted on every call.
byKey.d: A cached total goes wrong as soon as a score changes.

explain.text: Sorting 100,000 scores for each of 2,000 queries visits 200,000,000 scores. An ordered structure, updated on each score change, lets a query read 10 entries.

parts.question: Now add `reset(player)`, which sets a player's score to zero and removes the player from the board.

widget.how: Check runs this part's tests and part 1's tests again. A reset player leaves the board, even with a negative score.

feedback.correct: Pop the player from the dict.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is from part 1: `top` must still sum the highest scores.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 did not match. Trace it by hand.
byKey.test-5: Test 5: after players 1 and 2 are reset, `top(2)` reads the players that remain.
byKey.test-6: Test 6: a reset player leaves the board, so the later `top` calls sum fewer players.
byKey.test-7: Test 7: a reset player who scores again starts from zero.
byKey.test-8: Test 8: resetting a player who is not there changes nothing.
byKey.test-9: Test 9: the reset player is gone, not set to 0, so `top(2)` sums 10 and -3.

explain.text: `reset` removes the player's entry, so the next `top` cannot see the old score. A later `add_score` then starts from zero. Resetting a player who is not there changes nothing.

items.prose: A calendar takes 1,200 bookings, one at a time. Each `book` scans the whole list of earlier bookings, and an accepted booking is added to the list.

parts.question: In all, how many booking comparisons does the scan make?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first booking scans none and the last scans 1,199.

byKey.square: You multiplied 1,200 by 1,200. The list starts empty and grows.
byKey.once: You counted one scan. Each booking scans all earlier ones.

explain.text: Booking number $i$ compares with the $i$ bookings before it. The total is $0 + 1 + \dots + 1{,}199 = 1{,}200 \times 1{,}199 / 2 = 719{,}400$.

parts.question: Thousands of bookings arrive every second. What do you do for `k = 1`?

options.text: Keep bookings sorted and check the neighbours with `bisect`
Scan faster by writing the loop in a lower-level language, say C++
options.why: You kept the scan. It is still linear in the bookings so far.

options.text: Cache only the last booking and compare against it
options.why: You cached one booking. An earlier booking can still overlap a new one.

options.text: Sort the whole list again on every `book` call
options.why: You sorted every time. That costs more than the scan.

feedback.correct: A sorted list with `bisect` checks two neighbours.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which bookings can overlap a new one.

byKey.b: A faster scan is still a scan.
byKey.c: Only the neighbours in sorted order matter, not the latest booking.
byKey.d: Sorting is more work than scanning.

explain.text: Accepted bookings never overlap, so sorted order is time order. A new booking can only clash with its left and right neighbours. `bisect` finds them in $O(\log n)$.

parts.question: A binary search over 1,000,000 bookings needs how many comparisons at most, rounded up to a whole number?

widget.label: Comparisons
widget.accept: 20: the ceiling of log base 2 of 1,000,000

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each comparison halves the range.

byKey.half: You halved once. Each comparison halves the range again.
byKey.nineteen: $2^{19}$ is 524,288, which is below a million. You need 20.

explain.text: Each comparison halves the range, so $n$ bookings need $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ comparisons. Here $2^{19} = 524{,}288 < 10^6 < 2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$, so the answer is 20.

items.prose: Return the length of the longest contiguous stretch of `nums` that sums to 0, or 0 if none does. Values may be negative or zero. This code is correct but slow. It passes the small groups. Make the large group pass, in C++, as in l17.
items.question: Write a fast `longest_zero_sum_subarray` in C++.

tests.call: [&]{ std::vector<int> v; for (int i = 0; i < 150000; ++i) { v.push_back(2); v.push_back(-2); } return longest_zero_sum_subarray(v); }()
[&]{ std::vector<int> v; for (int i = 0; i < 120000; ++i) { v.push_back(3); v.push_back(1); v.push_back(-4); } v.push_back(6); return longest_zero_sum_subarray(v); }()

items.question: Say aloud how you would open a live round on `count_subarrays_divisible_by_k`.

widget.prompt: Say this aloud, timing yourself to six minutes, then write the main points. The problem is `count_subarrays_divisible_by_k`. Restate it and give an example. Name the brute force and its cost. Give the prefix-remainder idea, write the plan as comments and state the complexity. Use `[7, -2, 9, 4, -5, 6]` with `k = 5`.
widget.model:
**Restate.** Count the non-empty contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by `k`.

**Example.** For `[7, -2, 9, 4, -5, 6]` and `k = 5` the answer is 3. The prefix sums are 0, 7, 5, 14, 18, 13 and 19. Their remainders are 0, 2, 0, 4, 3, 3 and 4. Three pairs of prefixes share a remainder.

**Brute force.** Try every start and every end: $n(n + 1)/2$ subarrays. At $n = 300{,}000$ that is 45,000,150,000 steps, far too slow for a 5-second limit.

**Idea.** Two prefix sums with the same remainder differ by a multiple of `k`. So the stretch between them is divisible. Count, in a dict, the earlier prefixes with each remainder, starting with `{0: 1}`. Add that count at each step. In C++ fix a negative remainder with `((total + x) % k + k) % k`.

**Plan, as comments.** `# seen[r] = earlier prefixes with remainder r`, `# for each x: update remainder, add seen[r], then count it`, `# O(n) time, O(k) memory`.

**Complexity.** Linear time, and memory proportional to the number of distinct remainders, at most `k`.

rubric.text: Restates the problem and gives an example with its answer, 3
Names the brute force and its cost, 45,000,150,000 steps at 300,000
Gives the prefix-remainder idea: equal remainders bound a divisible subarray
States the plan before the code, including the dict started at {0: 1}
States linear time and memory by remainders, and the C++ negative remainder

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Mark your answer against the rubric.

explain.text: A good opening restates the problem and gives an example. It names the slow way with its cost, and states the idea before any code.

items.question: A leaderboard has 80,000 players and answers 1,500 `top(5)` queries. Sorting every score for each query visits how many scores in all?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each query sorts all 80,000 scores.

byKey.top: You counted the entries a maintained top 5 would touch. Sorting touches every score.
byKey.once: You counted one query. There are 1,500 of them.

explain.text: Each query sorts all 80,000 scores, so 1,500 queries visit $80{,}000 \times 1{,}500 = 120{,}000{,}000$. A maintained top 5 touches 5 entries a query, 7,500 in all. That is 16,000 times fewer.

items.question: A hidden test fails on time. Put the steps to a fix in order. Leave out the steps that do not belong.

lines.text: Note which test failed and how large its input is
Count the steps your code takes at that size
Name the line that takes most of them
Replace that line with a lookup or a sort
Rerun the failing test, then every other test
Print from every line and rerun the large test
lines.why: You added output to every line. That slows the code further and does not name the costly line.

lines.text: Submit anyway and hope the machine is faster
lines.why: You blamed the machine. The step count of your code is the cause.

feedback.correct: Find the size, count the steps, name the line, replace it, then rerun.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the one before it.

byKey.d1: Printing from every line does not name the costly one.
byKey.d2: A faster machine does not fix a code that takes too many steps.
byKey.left-out: Five steps belong. Printing everywhere and hoping do not.

explain.text: The failing test gives the size. The size gives the step count, and the steps point at the slow line. Only then does a rewrite help, and a full rerun confirms it.
